71.title: The changed word
71.hook: his son Ram Rai alters a word of Nanak's hymn to please the court, and the Guru refuses to see him again
71.howItsDone: Sikhs hold that the words of the Guru Granth Sahib must never be altered; the story of Ram Rai is told as the example of what happens when the word is changed to please power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the herb garden, and a cure sent to the emperor's son. Your line was heal whoever asks. Did you help someone without keeping score? Day seventy-one.

You're in a meeting with the most powerful person you've ever met. They quote something your grandmother used to say, and ask what it means. The honest answer might annoy them. You can see it in their face. So you shade it. Just one word. Just enough to keep the room happy. It's so easy. Everyone does it. It's called being diplomatic. Now imagine the thing you shaded wasn't your grandmother's saying. It was scripture. And the powerful person was the emperor. Today, the gentle seventh Guru draws the hardest line of his life, against his own son, over a single word.
screen: `THE MOST POWERFUL PERSON IN THE ROOM.` → `JUST ONE WORD, SHADED.` → `AND IT WAS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: By 1661 there was a new emperor, Aurangzeb, who had fought his way to the throne, and he summoned Guru Har Rai to Delhi. The Guru didn't go himself. He sent his elder son, Ram Rai, a bright young man, to answer for the community. At court, tradition says, Ram Rai impressed everyone. Then came a hard question. Someone pointed to a line in Guru Nanak's writing, in the long hymn called Asa di Var. The line says, in plain words, that the clay of a Muslim's grave ends up in the potter's hands, kneaded into pots and bricks. It's a reflection on death: whatever we believe about burial or cremation, the body becomes earth. The court heard it as an insult to Muslims. And Ram Rai, wanting to please, said it had been copied wrong. He changed the word Muslim to a word meaning a faithless person. It worked. The court was satisfied. When the news reached Kiratpur, the gentle Guru, the one who sent medicine even to the emperor's son, was unmoved. Tradition says he declared that Ram Rai had turned his back on the Guru's word, and he never saw his son again. He passed over him and chose his younger son, Har Krishan, as Guru. Why so hard, from so soft a man? Because for Sikhs, the word of the Gurus is not the Guru's to trade. You can be gentle with people. You can forgive enemies. But you don't edit what was given to please whoever holds power.
screen: `SUMMONED TO AURANGZEB'S COURT.` · `A LINE ABOUT CLAY AND THE POTTER.` · `RAM RAI CHANGES ONE WORD.` · `THE GURU NEVER SEES HIM AGAIN.` · then, large: `DON'T CHANGE THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one word you promised. Settle and breathe. Then bring to mind a promise you've made that's still open. To yourself, to a friend, to a child, to God if you pray. A small one is fine: I'll call. I'll come. I'll stop. Notice any way you've been quietly rewording it: I said I'd call, but a text counts. Just see it. Then let the original words stand, as they were said. The bell holds the time.
The changed word. Ram Rai altered one word of Guru Nanak's hymn to please the emperor's court, and his father never saw him again.
Your line: don't change the word. Today, keep the promise you thought of, in the words you first said it. Day seventy-one.

72.title: A Guru at five
72.hook: the youngest Guru takes up the task as a small child and is remembered for his calm
72.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, in the daily Ardas, asking that by remembering him all suffering may depart, and honor him as a picture of calm wisdom in a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the changed word: Ram Rai shaded one word for the court, and his father never saw him again. Your line was don't change the word. Did you keep your promise as you first said it? Day seventy-two.

Think of a five-year-old you know. They can tie a shoe, mostly. They can tell you, at length, about a dinosaur. They cry when the sandwich is cut the wrong way. Now picture that child being bowed to by grown men with long beards. Being asked to guide thousands of people. Being watched by an older brother who thinks the job should be his, and by an emperor who is curious what kind of child this is. That was Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, chosen in 1661 when his father, Guru Har Rai, died. Today, the youngest Guru, and what people remembered about him.
screen: `A FIVE-YEAR-OLD YOU KNOW.` → `BOWED TO BY GROWN MEN.` → `THE EIGHTH GURU.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Krishan became Guru at about five and lived only to about eight. So there are no great battles, no long books of hymns from him. What Sikhs remember is his calm, and what came out of it. His older brother Ram Rai, the one who changed the word, went to the emperor Aurangzeb and pressed his claim, and the child Guru was summoned to Delhi. On the way, tradition tells a story Sikhs love. At a village called Panjokhara, a proud scholar challenged the boy. If you're really the Guru, explain the Gita, the great Hindu scripture, to me. The Guru didn't argue, and didn't show off. Tradition says he asked for someone from the village, and a humble water-carrier named Chhajju was brought, a man who had never studied. The Guru touched him lightly with his stick, and Chhajju began to explain the Gita so deeply that the scholar was left silent, and humbled. The point isn't a trick. It's that wisdom was never about age or schooling; the child Guru pointed away from himself, to the least likely person in the village. In Delhi he stayed at the house of a Rajput noble, Raja Jai Singh. Tradition says the Raja's queen tested him by dressing as a maid among her servants, and the child walked straight to her. And tradition also says he declined to meet the emperor at all. Small, calm, unimpressed by the powerful. The youngest Guru.
screen: `GURU AT FIVE, GONE BY EIGHT.` · `SUMMONED TO DELHI.` · `CHHAJJU THE WATER-CARRIER.` · `CALM BEFORE THE POWERFUL.` · then, large: `SMALL, AND WISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing calmly. Pick something ordinary you're about to do anyway: pour a glass of water, fold a shirt, wash a cup. Before you start, take three slow breaths. Then do it at half speed, the way a small child does something important, with full attention and no hurry. Feel the weight of the cup, the sound of the water. When it's done, sit down again and let that calm spread into your breathing. The bell holds the time.
A Guru at five. Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, who led as a small child and is remembered for his calm and his humility.
Your line: small, and wise. Today, listen properly to the youngest or quietest person in the room, and let them teach you something. Day seventy-two.

73.title: Smallpox in Delhi
73.hook: he nurses the sick during an epidemic in Delhi and dies of it at eight, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands
73.howItsDone: Visitors to Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi often take water from its pool home for the sick, and Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan's care for the sick in the daily Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Guru at five, and Chhajju the water-carrier who explained the Gita. Your line was small, and wise. Who was the quiet teacher in your day? Day seventy-three.

Most of us remember what a city feels like when a sickness is loose in it. The empty streets. The fear of touching a door handle. Families keeping their distance from their own grandparents. And the people who went in anyway: nurses, cleaners, delivery drivers, neighbors carrying soup. In 1664, while the child Guru Har Krishan was staying in Delhi, an epidemic swept the city. Tradition names it smallpox, and some accounts add cholera. People were dying in the lanes. The eighth Guru was about seven years old, and a guest in a stranger's house. He could have left. Today, what a child did in a frightened city.
screen: `A CITY WITH A SICKNESS LOOSE.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO WENT IN ANYWAY.` → `DELHI, 1664.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the young Guru did not hide. He went among the sick of Delhi, Hindu and Muslim alike, comforting them and tending to them, and his followers with him. The house where he was staying, Raja Jai Singh's bungalow, had a well, and tradition says the Guru blessed its water and gave it to the sick. People came in crowds. Then the child caught the disease himself. Sikhs tell of his last days with great tenderness. He was burning with fever, and he stayed calm. His followers, frightened, asked who would lead them after him. Tradition says the dying boy gave a short, puzzling answer: Baba Bakale. The Baba, the next Guru, is at Bakala, a village in Punjab. He said no more. That riddle is tomorrow's story and the day after's. He died in Delhi in 1664, not yet eight years old. And here is what a visitor to Delhi can still see. The bungalow became Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, one of the best-known gurdwaras in the city. Beside it lies a large pool, fed, tradition says, from that same well, and people still take its water home to the sick. The langar there feeds huge numbers of people every day. During the COVID-19 pandemic, gurdwaras in Delhi, Bangla Sahib among them, cooked and delivered meals to people who couldn't leave home. A child's service in one epidemic, echoing in another, more than three hundred and fifty years later.
screen: `AMONG THE SICK OF DELHI.` · `WATER FROM THE WELL.` · `BABA BAKALE.` · `GURDWARA BANGLA SAHIB TODAY.` · then, large: `HE SERVED THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check on someone unwell. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is sick right now, in body or in spirit. A friend in the hospital. A parent with a long illness. Someone having a hard month. Hold them in your mind without trying to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, just wish them ease, breath by breath. And decide how you'll reach them today. The bell holds the time.
Smallpox in Delhi. In 1664 the child Guru Har Krishan tended the sick in an epidemic, caught it, and died, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands.
Your line: he served the sick. Today, reach out to the person you thought of: a call, a text, a meal left at the door. Day seventy-three.

74.title: The name of the sword
74.hook: Tyag Mal, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, fights so bravely he is called Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword
74.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, as both brave and deeply contemplative; his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, often about detachment and calm, are sung in gurdwaras and at Sikh funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, smallpox in Delhi, and the child Guru's last words: Baba Bakale. Your line was he served the sick. Did you reach the person you thought of? Day seventy-four.

Some people get their names twice. Once from their parents, and once from what they do. The kid everyone calls Doc because she bandaged the whole playground. The grandfather everyone calls Captain, though he never captained anything but the family. The second name tells you who a person became. The child Guru said the next Guru was at Bakala. To find out who he meant, we have to go back about thirty years, to Guru Hargobind's household, and to his youngest son, a quiet boy who got his second name on a battlefield. Today, a name that means a sword, given to a man who would spend most of his life in silence.
screen: `NAMED TWICE.` → `GURU HARGOBIND'S YOUNGEST SON.` → `A NAME FROM A BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: He was born in Amritsar in 1621, and his parents named him Tyag Mal. Tyag means renunciation, letting go. It suited him. He was thoughtful, inward, drawn to quiet. Then came the battles of Guru Hargobind's later years, the ones from day sixty-eight. At the battle of Kartarpur, in 1635, the boy was about thirteen or fourteen. Tradition says he fought with such courage and skill with the sword that afterward his father gave him a new name: Tegh Bahadur. Tegh is a sword. Bahadur means brave. Brave of the sword. You might expect a boy with a name like that to become a great commander. He did the opposite. After his father's death, he went with his mother, Mata Nanaki, and his wife, Mata Gujri, to Bakala, a village near the Beas, where his mother's family lived. And there, for about twenty years, he lived very quietly. Tradition says he spent long hours in meditation in a small room below ground, working with his hands, keeping to himself, while the Guruship passed to his nephew, Har Rai, and then to the child Har Krishan. Brave, then quiet. People who met the grown man found someone gentle and still, who wrote hymns of calm detachment, some of which are now in the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's the thing to carry. Courage doesn't always keep shouting. Sometimes the bravest people you know are the quietest, and their courage is simply waiting underneath, for the day it's needed.
screen: `TYAG MAL — LETTING GO.` · `KARTARPUR, 1635.` · `TEGH BAHADUR — BRAVE OF THE SWORD.` · `TWENTY QUIET YEARS AT BAKALA.` · then, large: `BRAVE, THEN QUIET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think where you were brave. Settle and breathe. Let one moment come back: a time you were more courageous than you expected. Maybe you spoke up. Maybe you stayed. Maybe you walked into a room you dreaded. It doesn't have to be dramatic. Feel it again in your body. Then notice how quiet that courage is now, sitting inside you, not needing to prove anything. Just rest with it. The bell holds the time.
The name of the sword. Tyag Mal fought so bravely as a boy that his father renamed him Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword.
screen: `THE NAME OF THE SWORD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: brave, then quiet. Today, do one brave thing without announcing it, and let nobody know but you. Day seventy-four.

75.title: Twenty-two claimants at Bakala
75.hook: tradition says the trader Makhan Shah found the true Guru meditating in Bakala among many false claimants
75.tomorrow: journeys east and a new town
75.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the story of Makhan Shah finding Guru Tegh Bahadur at Bakala, and his cry 'Guru ladho re', the Guru is found, is remembered at the gurdwara in Baba Bakala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name of the sword: Tyag Mal became Tegh Bahadur, then went quiet at Bakala. Your line was brave, then quiet. Did you do one brave thing without announcing it? Day seventy-five.

Search for almost anything online and you'll find a dozen people shouting that they're the real one. The original recipe. The authentic brand. The only true expert. The loudest voice gets the top of the page. Now picture the village of Bakala in 1664, after the child Guru's last words, Baba Bakale, reached Punjab. The next Guru is at Bakala. So, overnight, Bakala fills up with Gurus. Relatives of the Guru's family set up seats, gather followers, and announce themselves. Tradition says there were twenty-two of them. Somewhere in the village, a quiet man sits in a room below ground, saying nothing. Today, how the Sikhs found their Guru.
screen: `EVERYONE CLAIMS TO BE THE REAL ONE.` → `BAKALA FILLS WITH GURUS.` → `A QUIET MAN BELOW GROUND.`

segments.voice: The story Sikhs tell turns on a merchant named Makhan Shah, a trader who shipped goods by sea. Tradition says his ship was caught in a terrible storm, and in his fear he made a vow: if he reached land safely, he would give five hundred gold coins to the Guru. The ship survived. Makhan Shah came to Punjab to keep his promise, and arrived in Bakala to find twenty-two Gurus. How do you choose? He had a quiet plan. He went to each claimant in turn, bowed, and laid down just two gold coins. Each one accepted the coins, blessed him, and thanked him. None of them knew about the vow. Then someone told him there was one more: a man who lived simply, meditating in a small room, and made no claim at all. Makhan Shah went and found Tegh Bahadur, bowed, and laid down two coins. Tradition says the quiet man looked up and said, gently: you promised five hundred. The merchant knew. He ran up onto the roof and shouted out over the whole village, again and again: I've found the Guru! I've found the Guru! And so the man who had been brave, then quiet, became the ninth Guru. Here's what the story is doing. The real one wasn't the loudest. He wasn't even competing. He didn't tell Makhan Shah he was the Guru. He simply knew the truth of the man's heart. And the one who recognized him was not a scholar or a priest, but a trader who had kept his word.
screen: `A VOW IN A STORM AT SEA.` · `TWO COINS FOR EACH CLAIMANT.` · `YOU PROMISED FIVE HUNDRED.` · `SHOUTING FROM THE ROOF.` · then, large: `THE GURU IS FOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look past the loudest voice. Settle and breathe. Think of a question in your life right now where lots of voices are competing: a decision, a worry, a piece of news. Notice which voice is loudest, and set it aside for a moment. Then ask: is there a quieter voice here I've been walking past? A friend who said little. A feeling I haven't listened to. Your own sense of what's true. Just listen for it. The bell holds the time.
Twenty-two claimants at Bakala. Tradition says the trader Makhan Shah tested them all, and found the true Guru, Tegh Bahadur, meditating quietly.
Your line: the guru is found. Today, when you meet the quiet voice worth trusting, a person, a book, your own conscience, say so out loud. Day seventy-five.

76.title: Journeys east and a new town
76.word: Journeys east and a new town
76.hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur travels as far as Assam and founds the town that becomes Anandpur
76.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib, the town founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur, and gurdwaras mark his travels in the east, from Patna and Dhaka to Dhubri in Assam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twenty-two claimants at Bakala, and a trader shouting from the roof. Your line was the guru is found. Did you meet a quiet voice worth trusting? Day seventy-six.

Think of someone who started over. A family that moved to a new country with two suitcases and opened a shop. A friend who, after a hard year, bought a cheap old house and fixed it up one room at a time. Starting over takes a kind of courage that isn't loud at all. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the new ninth Guru, did not have an easy welcome. Some of the disappointed claimants turned hostile; tradition says one of them even had a shot fired at him. So the quiet Guru did two things. He built a new home. And he set out on the road, the longest journeys any Guru had made since Guru Nanak. Today, a town and a journey.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO STARTED OVER.` → `NOT AN EASY WELCOME.` → `A NEW HOME, AND THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the town. In 1665 the Guru bought a piece of land in the Shivalik foothills, near Kiratpur, from the local hill raja. He named the new settlement Chakk Nanaki, after his mother, Mata Nanaki. It was rough ground by the river Sutlej, with hills behind. Over the next years it would grow into a Sikh center known as Anandpur, the city of bliss. You met the word anand on day fifty-three, in the song of bliss. Anandpur would become one of the most important places in Sikh history; much of the rest of this camp happens there. Second, the journey. Soon after founding the town, the Guru set out east, the way Guru Nanak had gone long before, visiting Sikh communities and holy places. He traveled through Agra and Allahabad, to Benares, and on to Patna, on the Ganges. There he left his wife, Mata Gujri, who was expecting a child, and kept going: to Dhaka, in Bengal, and all the way to Assam, in the far east, where tradition says he helped make peace between an imperial army and the Assamese kingdom. While he was far away, in Patna, his son was born. The Guru would not see him for years. Here's the shape of it. The quiet man from the room below ground didn't wait for a perfect life. He took rough land and started a town. He took the road and strengthened scattered communities. Build where you are, with what you have, and let it grow into something you may never fully see.
screen: `CHAKK NANAKI, 1665.` · `ANANDPUR, THE CITY OF BLISS.` · `EAST AS FAR AS ASSAM.` · `A SON BORN IN PATNA.` · then, large: `BUILD WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant or start one small thing. Settle and breathe. Then think of something you've wanted to begin but keep saving for when life is calmer. A habit. A project. A friendship. A garden. Picture the rough ground as it is now, not ideal. Then picture the first small stake you could put in it, today, just one. If you have a seed, a pot, a notebook, you can even start it now, after the sit. For now, just hold the beginning. The bell holds the time.
Journeys east and a new town. Guru Tegh Bahadur founded Chakk Nanaki, which became Anandpur, and traveled east as far as Assam.
screen: `JOURNEYS EAST AND A NEW TOWN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: build where you are. Today, take the first small step on the thing you've been saving for later. Day seventy-six.

77.title: The pandits of Kashmir
77.hook: Kashmiri Brahmins facing forced conversion come to him for help
77.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of the Kashmiri pandits coming to Anandpur as the beginning of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, and honor him as one who gave his life for the freedom of others to practice their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, journeys east and a new town: Chakk Nanaki, the town that became Anandpur. Your line was build where you are. Did you take one first step? Day seventy-seven.

Look back at this week. A word changed to please a court. A child Guru, calm before the powerful, who served the sick and died in Delhi. A boy named brave of the sword who went quiet for twenty years. A trader shouting from a roof. A new town on rough ground. And now, spring of 1675, at Anandpur. The Guru is home, and his son, Gobind Rai, is about eight. A group of travelers arrives from the far north, from the valley of Kashmir, worn out from the mountain roads. They are pandits, Hindu Brahmin scholars and priests. They are not Sikhs. They've come a long way to ask a Guru for help. Today, the knock at the door.
screen: `A WEEK OF QUIET COURAGE.` → `ANANDPUR, 1675.` → `TRAVELERS FROM KASHMIR.`

segments.voice: Here is what the pandits told the Guru, as Sikh tradition remembers it. Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the Mughal governor of Kashmir was pressing Hindus there to convert to Islam, and the Brahmins, as religious leaders, were under the heaviest pressure. Tradition names their leader Pandit Kirpa Ram, from Mattan, near the town of Anantnag. They had nowhere else to turn. Historians discuss how widespread this policy was, and how the court saw it; the sources are not all agreed. What the Sikh sources agree on is the scene at Anandpur, and it's worth slowing down on what makes it remarkable. First, the pandits were not the Guru's followers. They wore the sacred thread and the forehead mark, practices the Gurus themselves had not taken up. Guru Nanak, as a boy, had famously declined to wear the thread. Second, the Guru's own community was not being threatened in this request. He could have said: this isn't our fight. Third, the Guru listened. Tradition says he sat quietly for a long time, deep in thought, heavy with what they had told him. The question in the air was simple and terrible: who would stand up for the right of other people to practice a faith that wasn't his? Tomorrow and the days after, we'll see his answer, and what it cost. Today, notice only this. The people in need came to him, and he did not send them away.
screen: `PRESSURE TO CONVERT IN KASHMIR.` · `PANDIT KIRPA RAM LEADS THEM.` · `NOT HIS FOLLOWERS, NOT HIS THREAD.` · `THE GURU SITS AND LISTENS.` · then, large: `THEY CAME TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone asking for help. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has come to you lately, even in a small way: a message you skimmed, a friend who said I'm fine too quickly, a coworker who needed more than they asked for. Replay it slowly. This time, just listen. Don't plan your answer. Notice what they were really asking. Stay with them, the way the Guru sat with the travelers. The bell holds the time.
The pandits of Kashmir. Hindu scholars under pressure to convert, who traveled to Anandpur in 1675 to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help.
Your line: they came to him. Today, when someone comes to you, stop what you're doing and really listen, even for two minutes. Day seventy-seven, the end of another week.
